title: Hold or release: is the break ready?
outcomes: Counts how many White pawns attack d5 before and after a pawn push and says whether the push releases the bind
As the cramped side, checks whether the pawn that would stand on b5 has a defender before choosing ...b5
Chooses between holding the bind, a quiet move and a trade in positions where nobody names the plan
Recognises a position that is not the bind at all

steps.text: In **The Maroczy bind: what it holds back, and what it costs** you met the bind and its price. Now decide in a position: should the owner hold it or release it, and is the cramped side's break ready? A pawn push by the owner changes how many White pawns attack d5 and b5. Count first. Rule of thumb: hold the bind unless a push wins something concrete.

steps.caption: White to move. Two White pawns (c4, e4) attack d5. The push c5 would be a way to release the bind.

line.say: c5 leaves e4 as the only pawn attacking d5: the grip on d5 is halved.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The cramped side's break is ready when the pawn that makes it has a defender for each attacker. A pawn on b5 is attacked by c4; a Black pawn on a6 defends it. A pawn on d5 is attacked by c4 and e4 and needs two defenders. Pieces behind the break matter too.

steps.title: Same bind, the same break
steps.prompt: Predict for each position whether ...b5 is a reasonable move. In the second, one Black pawn is on another square; in the third, one White rook is.
Before you play ...b5 or ...d5 in a bind next time, write the number of attackers and the number of defenders of the break square. Which count do you expect to forget more often?
